opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think commoditization is real, but it's happening unevenly, and that unevenness is where the value is.

Structure prediction is the clearest example. A few years ago, getting a high-quality predicted structure was a genuine moat. Now there are several open models that are good enough for most everyday use, and the marginal value of being slightly better on a benchmark has collapsed. If your whole business was "we predict structures," that's a hard place to be.

Design is different, because the bottleneck isn't the model, it's the loop. Generating a plausible binder or enzyme scaffold is increasingly cheap. Knowing which of the ten thousand candidates will express, fold, stay stable, avoid immunogenicity, and actually work in a cell is still hard. That knowledge comes from wet-lab data, and especially from negative data, the stuff that failed, which almost nobody publishes. So I'd argue the frontier model itself depreciates fast, but the data flywheel around it doesn't.

There are a couple of implications. First, the value shifts from model weights to closed-loop systems: design, synthesize, test, retrain, in tight cycles. Whoever runs that loop fastest, on the properties that actually matter commercially, has the durable advantage. Second, frontier models still matter at the edges, on the problems open models can't do yet: multi-state design, conformational dynamics, designing function rather than just shape. That frontier keeps moving, so being first there is valuable, but it's a temporary lead you have to keep renewing.

And third, commoditization is honestly good for the field. When the base capabilities are cheap, many more groups can try ideas, and the interesting work moves up the stack toward specific therapeutic or industrial problems. The analogy I like is compute: nobody wins because they have a CPU, they win because of what they build and the proprietary feedback they get from users. In protein design, the "users" are the assays.

So my short answer: the models are commoditizing, the problems aren't. Value accrues to whoever owns the hard-to-get experimental signal and can turn it into better designs faster than everyone else.

astra-6.text:
I think commoditization shifts where the value sits. If everyone has access to a strong protein design model, then generating a candidate becomes cheaper, and the model itself becomes harder to differentiate on. But generating a candidate isn’t the same as getting a protein that works.

The value moves toward knowing what to design, having the experimental infrastructure to test it, and feeding those results back into the next round. Two teams can use the same model and get very different outcomes because they have different data and different feedback loops.

So frontier models can still be valuable, especially if they unlock something you couldn’t do before. The question is how long that advantage lasts—and whether you can turn it into experimental results and useful products before the rest of the field catches up.

r001.rationale: The response discusses commoditization and experimental feedback, but does not say that overall LLM market growth lets closed-source frontier models retain most of the value as open-source models gain share.

sol-6.1.text:
I think commoditization shifts where the value accrues. If everyone has access to a model that can generate plausible proteins, then generating a sequence becomes less of a differentiator. The harder question is whether that protein actually does what you need it to do.

Frontier models can still be valuable if they meaningfully improve your probability of success or let you tackle something that was previously out of reach. But that advantage has to translate into experimental results. Otherwise, as models get cheaper and more widely available, the value moves toward proprietary data, experimental validation, and the ability to learn from failures. It’s the loop between design and experiment that becomes really important.
